client: I've been feeling really anxious lately because I failed two important exams this semester. I'm worried I won't be able to catch up and graduate on time, and the thought of being behind all my classmates makes me panic. To be honest, I'm not sure talking about it will help - the deadlines and requirements aren't going to change just because I feel bad about them.
therapist: It sounds like you're carrying a heavy load of worry about these exams and what they mean for your future. The fear of falling behind can feel overwhelming, especially when comparing yourself to others. What thoughts go through your mind when you imagine not graduating on time?

client: I keep picturing myself still sitting in classes next year while all my friends are moving on to jobs or grad school. It makes me feel like such a failure - like I'm not smart enough to keep up. Even when I study for hours, I still blank out during tests and then beat myself up about it afterward.
therapist: I hear how painful this comparison is for you, and how much self-doubt is coming up around your abilities. That cycle of studying hard but struggling in tests sounds frustrating and disheartening. What evidence do you have about times when you *have* been able to perform well academically?

client: I guess there were a few times I did okay on quizzes last semester, but those don't really count because they were so much easier than the big exams. I just feel like when it really matters, I always choke under pressure. Even thinking about those small successes makes me anxious because it reminds me how inconsistent I am.
therapist: It sounds like you're discounting those smaller successes while putting tremendous pressure on yourself to perform perfectly when it "really matters." That all-or-nothing thinking must make exams feel incredibly high-stakes. How do you think this pressure affects your ability to focus when taking important tests?

client:
You know, I never really thought about it that way, but you're right. The pressure does make it so much harder to focus during exams. My mind just goes blank sometimes, or I start second-guessing every answer. It's like I'm so afraid of failing that I can't even think straight. 

But at the same time, I don't know how to stop putting this pressure on myself. These tests do matter a lot for my future, so shouldn't I be taking them seriously? I feel like if I relax too much, I'll just end up doing worse.
therapist:
I hear that tension between knowing the pressure hurts your performance, yet feeling like you *should* be stressed because the stakes are high. That's such a difficult spot to be in.  

What would it look like to take these exams seriously *without* that overwhelming pressure - is there a middle ground you can imagine between total panic and complete relaxation?

client:
I don’t know if a middle ground exists for me. When I try to relax even a little, my brain screams that I’m being lazy and will fail. The pressure feels like the only thing keeping me going, even though I know it makes my mind go blank during tests.  

I guess the idea of balancing seriousness and calm sounds nice, but it just feels impossible right now. How am I supposed to care enough to study but not care enough to panic? That doesn’t make sense to me.
therapist:
I can hear how stuck you feel between these two extremes - either paralyzed by pressure or afraid that any relaxation means you're not trying hard enough. That all-or-nothing thinking is making this so much harder for you.  

What if we explored how other people you respect manage to prepare seriously *without* that overwhelming panic? Who comes to mind as someone who works hard but doesn't seem to torture themselves like this?

client:
Hmm, I guess my friend Mark comes to mind—he always seems prepared but never looks as stressed as I do. But comparing myself to him just makes me feel worse because I think "he must be smarter" or "he doesn't care as much as I do." 

I get what you're saying about all-or-nothing thinking, but it's hard to imagine finding a middle ground. If I'm not panicking, I worry I'm being lazy or naive about how much work this really takes.
therapist:
It sounds like even thinking about Mark's approach brings up those harsh comparisons and self-judgments again. You're caught between admiring his calmness and fearing that if you're not stressed, you're not doing enough—that's such a painful bind.  

What do you think would happen if, just for one study session, you experimented with Mark's level of calm *without* assuming it means you care less? Could we explore what that might look like?

client: I don't know... even the idea of trying to be calm like Mark makes me anxious. What if I *do* end up caring less? My grades already feel shaky, and if I relax too much, I'm scared I'll fall behind completely. It's like my stress is the only thing keeping me on track.
therapist:
I hear how scary it is to imagine loosening that grip of stress—it feels like the only thing holding everything together right now. That fear of spiraling if you ease up even a little must make it so hard to consider another way.  

What if, instead of trying to be calm like Mark right away, we started smaller—what’s one tiny way you could test if stress *truly* equals effort for you? For example, scheduling a 5-minute break during your next study session without judging yourself?

client: I get what you're saying about starting small, but even five minutes feels risky. What if I lose my momentum and can't get back into studying? I've had that happen before where I took a short break and then couldn't focus for hours afterward. The stress kind of keeps me on track, you know?
therapist:
It makes sense that you're wary of breaks when you've had experiences where they disrupted your focus instead of refreshing you. That fear of losing control over your productivity is really holding you in this stressful cycle.  

What if we approach this differently—instead of a break, could we experiment with just noticing when the stress peaks during studying, without trying to change it yet? Just becoming aware might help us understand how stress actually affects your focus.

client: I get what you're saying, but when I notice the stress building up, it just makes me panic more because I can feel myself losing control. Like last week, I started noticing my heart racing while studying, and then I completely spiraled about wasting time. Isn't paying attention to it just going to make it worse?
therapist:
It sounds like noticing your stress actually intensifies it right now—like shining a light on it makes the panic grow instead of easing it. That makes complete sense when stress feels so out of control.  

What do you think happens if, instead of focusing on the stress itself, we gently redirect to your physical surroundings for just 10 seconds when you notice tension rising? For example, naming three objects you can see in the room?

client:
I get what you're saying, but when I'm really anxious, it's like my brain is screaming too loud to notice anything around me. The other day I tried counting objects during a panic attack, and I just kept losing track because my thoughts were racing so fast. It made me feel even more frustrated with myself. 

Also, sometimes focusing on my surroundings makes me hyper-aware of how alone I am in the room, which just makes the loneliness worse. I know you're trying to help, but simple techniques like this often feel too small for how big the anxiety gets.
therapist:
It sounds like these well-meaning techniques sometimes end up highlighting just how overwhelming and isolating the anxiety feels—almost like trying to put a small bandage on a deep wound. That frustration when nothing seems to meet the enormity of what you're feeling must be exhausting.  

Instead of trying to "fix" the anxiety right now, would it feel more helpful to simply acknowledge together how relentless it is in those moments? What does it *need* from you when it gets that loud?
